# King's Scholar: Concise Summary
## Historical Origins and Definition
The title "King's Scholar" originated in 1317 when King Edward II sent 12 boys from his household to study at Cambridge. In 1440, King Henry VI founded Eton College, establishing 70 King's Scholars who received free education and lived in the College building, distinguished from fee-paying students ("Oppidans"). At Eton, King's Scholars (also called "Collegers" or "tugs") currently gain admission through competitive examination ("College Election"), receive Foundation Scholarships, and are housed in the historical College premises. They wear distinctive black academic gowns and participate in unique traditions, such as dining in College Hall and extended participation in the Wall Game. Historically, scholarships fully waived school fees, but now waivers are means-tested. King's Scholars append "KS" after their surnames in college lists.

# King's Scholar: Concise Summary
## Other Institutions
The designation also applies at Westminster School (where the title switches to Queen’s Scholar if a female monarch reigns), selected by examination and housed in College, wearing gowns at Abbey services. At King's College Cambridge, King's Scholars are undergraduates who achieve a first-class degree, awarded a prize and honored in a chapel ceremony. The seven King's Schools re-endowed by Henry VIII (Canterbury, Chester, Ely, Gloucester, Peterborough, Rochester, Worcester) use King's Scholarship to honor academic or musical attainment, with traditional privileges (such as marriage or burial rights in affiliated cathedrals), and since 1973 also award Queen’s Scholarships to female scholars. Notable traditions include the "Hoop Trundle" at King’s Ely and ceremonial admission services at both Ely and Canterbury.
